newsitem.title: UK: New surgery saves women's breasts, esteem.
newsitem.headline: New surgery saves women's breasts, esteem.

text.p: Millions of women could be saved from humiliating disfigurement after breast cancer surgery thanks to a new technique, plastic surgeons in Britain reported on Tuesday.
They teamed up with cancer surgeons in a dual operation that removed the cancerous tumour from the breast and immediately replaced it with muscle and skin from the woman's back.

"We...decided to stop the mutilation of women's breasts," CC Koo, a plastic surgeon at Stoke Mandeville hospital in Aylesbury, England told a news conference. "No woman should have to suffer...deformity after breast cancer."
Koo told a meeting of the British Association of Plastic Surgeons that she and colleagues had tried out the technique successfully on 40 women.
She showed photographs of patients with scars barely showing on the breasts, and compared these to women whose breasts were severely deformed after breast cancer surgery.

Koo said the new technique was becoming more possible as doctors had moved away from radical mastectomies -- which remove the entire breast as well as surrounding lymph glands -- to lumpectomies, which remove just the tumour.
But even lumpectomies could cause disfigurement.
"If you take away skin from the breast and do not restore it, you are bound to distort the breast," Koo said. "People are just now beginning to realise that it does cause deformity."

During the operation, the women is kept on her side so both the breast and her back are accessible. The cancer surgeon removes the lump and the plastic surgeon moves in immediately to take a comparably sized piece of muscle and skin from the back and stitch it into place on the breast.
The muscle used, the latissimus dorsi, was not vital to most women's movement. "It's a muscle that's important if you are a champion climber," Koo said.
The muscular back is also less prone to distort into a horrible scar than the soft breast tissue.
The operation took an average of two hours and patients left hospital after a week. Total reconstruction of the breast took four to six hours and required a two-week hospital stay.
She said 80 percent of women who had breast cancer were candidates for the new surgical technique, which she said had no serious side-effects.

Koo said as far as she knew, her team was the first to report using such a technique. The women who took part were now undergoing a psychological study to see how much their self-esteem had been boosted.
She said doctors were starting to realise that disfigurement could be more upsetting than having the entire breast removed -- and that cosmetic issues were more than just vanity.
Women in Western industrialised countries such as Britain have a one in 12 chance of developing breast cancer.
